A content delivery network solves a simple problem: the computer that originally holds a website's files, called the origin server, might sit far away, so every visit takes a while to load. Instead of forcing every request to travel that full distance, copies of the content get stored on servers scattered closer to people, at what's called an edge location. When someone requests a page and the nearby copy is already there and ready, that's a cache hit, meaning the answer came back fast without bothering the distant original at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries stocking popular books so nobody has to travel to the one national archive every time they want to read something. If a particular edge location doesn't have a fresh copy, it quietly fetches one from the origin server, stores it, and serves it locally from then on, so the next reader benefits immediately. This is why streaming video starts almost instantly, why online stores load quickly during busy shopping periods, and why a website stays reachable even when a huge crowd shows up at once. The system spreads out the demand instead of piling it all onto one machine.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the real, master copy of a website's content | Everything ultimately comes from here if no closer copy exists |
| Edge location | A server placed physically closer to everyday users | Shorter distance means faster loading times |
| Cache hit | A successful case where a nearby copy answers the request | Avoids a slow trip back to the origin server |
| Content delivery network | The whole system of connected edge locations working together | Keeps websites fast and reliable no matter how many people visit at once |
